Dictionaries_Code_Medium_1: Combine items from two separate inventory mappings so quantities for shared items aggregate together.

When processing each item from the second inventory, retrieve its current quantity in the merged store (defaulting to zero if absent), add the incoming count, and store the updated sum.
Dictionaries_MCQ_Hard_1: Consider the algorithmic performance of hash table data structures.
In the absence of excessive hash collisions, computing a key's hash allows direct indexing into memory buckets.
Identify the standard big-O complexity that represents constant-time operations for lookups, insertions, and deletions.
Dictionaries_MCQ_Hard_2: Review the evolution of dictionary implementation details from Python 3.6 to Python 3.7.
Prior to Python 3.7, dictionaries were officially considered unordered mappings.
Python 3.7 formalized that dictionaries are guaranteed to maintain the exact order in which keys were inserted.
Dictionaries_MCQ_Hard_3: Review modern operators introduced in Python 3.9 for dictionary manipulation.
Python 3.9 introduced binary operators for merging two dictionaries into a new mapping.
Identify the pipe symbol operator borrowed from set operations that combines two dictionaries, giving precedence to right-hand keys.
Dictionaries_SA_Hard_1: Explain how CPython dictionaries convert keys into array indices using internal hash functions.
Describe collision resolution strategies such as open addressing with perturbation to search for alternative table slots.
Discuss modern compact dictionary layout: separating a sparse hash index table from a dense array of entries to optimize memory.
Dictionaries_Code_Hard_1: Initialize an empty dictionary where original values will serve as keys and lists of original keys will serve as values.
Iterate through the input dictionary's key-value pairs.
For each value, append the corresponding key to the grouped list associated with that value in the result mapping, and return the inverted dictionary.
File Handling_MCQ_Easy_1: Recall the standard built-in function used to open file descriptors on disk in Python.
It accepts a file path string and access mode flags, returning a file stream object.
Identify the short built-in function name that opens a file for input or output.
File Handling_MCQ_Easy_2: Review the file mode flags used with open(): 'r', 'w', 'a', 'b', 't'.
When the mode parameter is omitted, consider whether Python defaults to reading or writing.
The default mode opens the file for reading content in standard text mode.
File Handling_MCQ_Easy_3: Review how context managers handle system resource lifecycles.
Manual file handling requires explicit close() calls that may be skipped if an unexpected exception occurs.
The 'with' statement guarantees that the file stream is closed automatically upon exiting the block, even if errors occur.
File Handling_SA_Easy_1: Explain the standard lifecycle of file handling: opening with proper mode, performing I/O, and ensuring resource closure.
Contrast the primary access modes: 'r' for reading, 'w' for overwriting/creating, and 'a' for appending.
Emphasize the advantage of using context managers ('with open') to automatically manage file descriptors and prevent leaks.
File Handling_Code_Easy_1: First open the file in write mode using a context manager and write the provided text content to disk.
Next, open the same file in read mode using a context manager to retrieve its contents.
Read the stored text from the file stream and return the resulting string.
File Handling_MCQ_Medium_1: Contrast write mode with append mode when opening an existing file.
Mode 'w' resets the file length to zero upon opening, removing any existing content.
Mode 'a' positions the file cursor at the end of existing contents, writing new data without erasing previous lines.
File Handling_MCQ_Medium_2: Compare file reading methods: read(), readline(), and readlines().
Notice the plural naming of readlines(), indicating it processes all lines in the file stream.
It returns a list of strings where each element represents a single line including its trailing newline character.
File Handling_MCQ_Medium_3: Understand how file stream pointers track the current read/write position within an open file.
Calling seek() adjusts the byte offset of the file pointer.
Passing an offset of 0 repositions the cursor back to the very beginning of the file.
File Handling_SA_Medium_1: Compare how read(), readline(), and line iteration handle memory when reading files.
Explain that read() loads the entire file into memory at once, while readline() reads a single line per call.
Highlight that direct file iteration ('for line in f:') streams chunks lazily through a buffer, providing optimal memory efficiency for large files.
File Handling_Code_Medium_1: Open the specified file in write mode and write each log line followed by a newline character.
Open the file in read mode, iterate through the lines, and check for the presence of target log indicators (such as 'ERROR').
Count the matching occurrences and return the final count.
File Handling_MCQ_Hard_1: Consider how operating systems determine default character encodings when opening text files.
When encoding is omitted, Python falls back to system locale settings, which differ between Windows, macOS, and Linux.
Specifying UTF-8 explicitly guarantees consistent cross-platform decoding and prevents unexpected UnicodeDecodeError exceptions.
File Handling_MCQ_Hard_2: Review the special dunder methods that implement Python's context management protocol.
One method executes when entering the with block to set up the resource, and another executes upon exit.
Identify the matching dunder method pair that handles setup and teardown for context managers.
File Handling_MCQ_Hard_3: Consider the system performance cost of invoking direct operating system read/write system calls.
Frequent unbuffered I/O operations trigger expensive kernel context switches and disk controller interrupts.
Buffering aggregates multiple small operations into larger in-memory chunks before flushing to disk, significantly boosting throughput.
File Handling_SA_Hard_1: Explain the responsibilities of `__enter__` and `__exit__` in implementing context management.
Describe the three exception arguments received by `__exit__`: exception type, exception value, and traceback object.
Explain how returning True from `__exit__` suppresses an exception, while returning False allows it to propagate upward normally.
File Handling_Code_Hard_1: Write the raw CSV string data to the specified file path using a text file context manager.
Read the file back using Python's standard csv module (such as csv.reader or csv.DictReader) to parse rows.
Compute the required summary metrics (such as row count or column totals) from the parsed rows and return the summary dictionary.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Easy_1: Recall the compound statement structure used to handle runtime errors in Python.
Risky code is placed inside the 'try' block, followed by the block that catches specific errors.
Identify the keyword that defines the error-handling clause for anticipated exception types.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Easy_2: Review the four clauses of a try-except statement: try, except, else, and finally.
Consider which block is designed specifically for mandatory cleanup tasks regardless of execution outcome.
This block executes unconditionally, whether the try block succeeded, caught an error, or raised an unhandled exception.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Easy_3: Recall how Python programs trigger or throw exceptions intentionally.
In Python, exceptions are activated using a dedicated statement keyword followed by an exception instance or class.
Look for the five-letter keyword that raises an exception into the active call stack.
Exception Handling_SA_Easy_1: Explain how structured exception handling prevents programs from crashing when unexpected runtime events occur.
Describe the role of 'try' for isolating risky code, 'except' for handling specific failures gracefully, and 'finally' for cleanup.
Emphasize that 'finally' executes unconditionally, ensuring resources like files or database connections are released.
Exception Handling_Code_Easy_1: Place the arithmetic division operation inside a try block.
Add an except clause specifically for ZeroDivisionError and another for TypeError.
Return the expected error message strings for zero division or type errors, and return the quotient on successful division.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Medium_1: Analyze the purpose of the optional 'else' block in a try-except structure.
Contrast the 'else' block with the 'except' block (runs on error) and the 'finally' block (runs always).
The else block executes only when the code inside the try block runs to completion without raising any exceptions.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Medium_2: Review how multiple exception types are grouped together in a single except clause.
When specifying multiple exception classes in one clause, Python requires them to be enclosed in a specific container.
Look for the syntax that encloses the comma-separated exception classes inside parentheses as a tuple.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Medium_3: Consider Python's built-in exception inheritance hierarchy.
BaseException is reserved for system-level signals like KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit that should rarely be caught.
Standard user-defined exceptions and library errors should inherit from the standard built-in Exception class.
Exception Handling_SA_Medium_1: Contrast the execution conditions of 'else' (runs only on zero errors) with 'finally' (runs unconditionally).
Explain that catching specific exceptions prevents masking unrelated programming bugs like NameError or typos.
Emphasize that broad exception catching inadvertently intercepts critical system signals like KeyboardInterrupt.
Exception Handling_Code_Medium_1: Initialize a list for successfully converted integers and an error counter initialized to zero.
Iterate through the string items and attempt integer conversion inside a try block.
Catch ValueError when conversion fails to increment the error counter without crashing, and return a dictionary with the results.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Hard_1: Consider what types of exceptions are caught when using a bare except clause without specifying an exception class.
A bare except intercepts all subclasses of BaseException, including system exit requests.
This intercepts KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C) and SystemExit, preventing users and operating systems from stopping the program cleanly.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Hard_2: Review exception chaining syntax introduced in Python 3.
The 'from' clause links a new high-level exception to an underlying root-cause exception.
It explicitly sets the `__cause__` attribute, preserving the original error context in the resulting traceback.
Exception Handling_MCQ_Hard_3: Trace execution flow when a function reaches a return statement inside a try block followed by a finally block.
The finally block is guaranteed to execute before the function actually exits, even if a return has been encountered.
If the finally block executes its own return statement, it overrides and discards any return value queued by the try block.
Exception Handling_SA_Hard_1: Outline the hierarchy rooted at BaseException, noting that Exception inherits from it while SystemExit and KeyboardInterrupt do not.
Contrast implicit exception chaining (via `__context__`) with explicit chaining (via `raise ... from ...` setting `__cause__`).
Explain how preserving the causal chain assists debugging while catching BaseException breaks standard runtime signaling.
Exception Handling_Code_Hard_1: Use a loop running up to max_retries attempts.
Inside the loop, call func() within a try-except block; if it succeeds, return the resulting value immediately.
If an exception occurs on each attempt and all retries are exhausted, return the fallback value or raise the error.
